title: Course Listing Unavailable

jokes.text: Alex Osbourne's video will: 'If you're watching this, it means I'm dead. Or I'm just showing you. Uh, but I'm probably dead.'
jokes.setup: Classic dramatic video will opening — 'If you're watching this, I'm dead' — sets up a grave, serious tone.
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts it with the mundane possibility that he's just showing it to someone, then resignedly commits back to the original premise.
jokes.explanation: A sharp, economical subversion of a cliché opening. The pivot to 'or I'm just showing you' is funny because it's so casually considered, and 'but I'm probably dead' landing as a resigned shrug is excellent deadpan structure. Scores high on craft because the joke is tight and the misdirection is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: If you're watching this, I'm dead.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Just kidding, I'm fine.

jokes.text: Star-Burns' will: 'To my ex-wife Magda, I leave herpes. But she knows that, it's dealt with.'
jokes.setup: Formal will reading format creates expectation of sentimental or monetary bequests.
jokes.punchline: He bequeaths herpes, then immediately clarifies it's already been transmitted and medically addressed — treating a horrifying overshare as bureaucratic housekeeping.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The formal will structure makes the herpes reveal genuinely shocking, and 'but she knows that, it's dealt with' is a perfect pivot — reframing a crude shock as a matter-of-fact administrative update. The economy is exceptional: five words defuse the shock into something even funnier. Fully character-specific to a low-status loser like Star-Burns. Earns its 8+ because the layering (shock → deflation → character revelation) is genuinely well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: My grandfather left me his entire estate. His house, his car, his life savings... and apparently his STD.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: The lawyer said it's been in the family for three generations.

jokes.text: Star-Burns leaves his Styx album collection 'to no one. Because that's who appreciated Styx as much as me.'
jokes.setup: Continuation of the will; he's about to leave cherished possessions to loved ones.
jokes.punchline: He leaves his Styx collection to no one — not as an insult to anyone, but because no one on earth shares his appreciation. Delivered as genuine pathos.
jokes.explanation: Works because it's both a joke about Styx's uncoolness AND a surprisingly poignant portrait of Star-Burns as a lonely man whose tastes nobody shares. The double meaning (no one appreciates Styx; no one appreciated me) gives it emotional depth without being sappy. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: I'm leaving my prized possession in my will.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: My complete Styx collection.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Who are you leaving it to?

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: I haven't decided yet. I'm going to wait and see who dies first, then give it to someone else.

jokes.text: The group receives the tape: 'Some one-armed guy with a scar on his face dropped it off. He said he was Star-Burns' lawyer.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks where the mysterious video came from
jokes.punchline: A one-armed, scarred man claiming to be Star-Burns' lawyer delivered it — an absurdly cinematic detail for a community college meth cook
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist worldbuilding — the idea that Star-Burns had a dramatic lawyer worthy of a thriller movie is a funny gap between his actual status and this grandiose delivery system.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, so how does a one-armed lawyer argue a case?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He doesn't. He just points.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's not funny.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, but this is.

jokes.text: Abed asks how one-armed the lawyer was; Troy demonstrates and says 'it was the other arm.'
jokes.setup: Abed learns Star-Burns' will was delivered by a one-armed man with a scar. He asks 'how one-armed was he? Tell me when to stop.'
jokes.punchline: Troy presumably demonstrates by hiding one arm progressively, and says 'it was the other arm' — suggesting the missing arm is the unexpected one, implying perhaps a very specific prosthetic or the wrong arm is functional.
jokes.explanation: A quick, visual bit that works partly because of Abed's absurd precision ('tell me when to stop') and Troy's deadpan response. The joke lives in the physical performance and the absurdity of treating arm-amputation level as a measurable spectrum. Rewatch bonus because the visual of the demonstration is probably funnier than the line alone.

dialogue.line: Continuation of the literal demonstration

jokes.text: Remark that Star-Burns 'died how he lived... in a meth lab explosion.'
jokes.setup: Abed wants help writing obituary copy. Jeff begins the classic 'died how he lived' trope.
jokes.punchline: The expected ending is something poetic or ironic (e.g., 'alone,' 'loudly'); instead it's the literal cause of death — a meth lab explosion — delivered as if it's both tragic AND perfectly on-brand.
jokes.explanation: Economically perfect. The 'died how he lived' formula creates a strong expectation, and the literal payoff subverts it completely while also being exactly right for Star-Burns. High quotability because it's self-contained and re-deployable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Here lies Pierce Hawthorne. He died how he lived: in a meth lab explosion.

jokes.text: 'He's in a better place now.' / 'Yeah. The blu-ray shelf.'
jokes.setup: Pierce offers the standard comfort cliché: 'He's in a better place now.' This normally means heaven.
jokes.punchline: Abed recontextualizes it literally and materially — Star-Burns is now on Abed's blu-ray shelf as a tribute video, which Abed considers an upgrade.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best quick jokes. Completely Abed-specific — only he would literalize a spiritual cliché in terms of media archiving, and only he would sincerely consider a blu-ray shelf a 'better place.' The setup/subversion is immaculate, and the economy is perfect. Earns its 8+ because the joke is fully character-integrated and the subversion is unexpected while being totally logical for Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: When my husband passed, I found comfort in knowing he was in a better place.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, that shelf is pretty nice. Good lighting, dust-free.

jokes.text: Star-Burns left Abed his ashes, with a request that they 'be burnt.' Abed: 'I don't think he knows how ashes work.'
jokes.setup: Abed reveals Star-Burns left instructions for his ashes to be burned.
jokes.punchline: Abed points out the logical impossibility — ashes are what remain after burning; you can't burn them again. Star-Burns fundamentally misunderstood his own end-of-life arrangement.
jokes.explanation: Tight and funny. The joke operates on two levels: Star-Burns is dumb enough to not understand cremation, and Abed is literal-minded enough to notice and report it clinically. The deadpan delivery ('I don't think he knows how ashes work') is pitch-perfect Community.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You can't burn ashes. They're already burned. That's what ashes are.

jokes.text: 'The small one's his lizard. If we rub that, will he come out and do celebrity impressions?'
jokes.setup: Two urns are presented — one for Star-Burns and one, presumably, for his lizard.
jokes.punchline: Troy treats the lizard urn like a magic lamp and asks if rubbing it will summon the lizard to do celebrity impressions — a completely invented, non-sequitur ability for the lizard.
jokes.explanation: Classic Troy absurdism — the genie-lamp logic applied to funeral urns, plus the random specificity of 'celebrity impressions' as the lizard's talent. Funny but slightly underbaked; the celebrity impressions addition feels a bit arbitrary even for Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Why is there a tiny lamp next to the urn?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not a lamp, Pierce. That's the urn.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, rub it and make a wish!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Pierce, that's a cremated lizard.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Three wishes, lizard. Don't be stingy.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Then I want it out of here.' (In response to learning the lizard urn can't do celebrity impressions.)
jokes.setup: Troy asks if rubbing the lizard urn would produce celebrity impressions. Abed says no.
jokes.punchline: Pierce, who has been listening, immediately decides the urn has no value and demands it removed. His threshold for keeping a dead classmate's lizard ashes is apparently 'can it do impressions.'
jokes.explanation: Pierce's bluntness and self-centeredness are perfectly distilled here — he only tolerates things that entertain him. Fast reaction beat that lands because Pierce's callousness is so consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, are you pregnant? Because I have a guy who can help with that. No questions asked.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Is it always about the Holocaust with you people?' — in response to someone wanting to discuss 'this really serious thing that's happened.'
jokes.setup: Someone opens a somber conversation about 'this really serious thing.' The audience expects Star-Burns discussion.
jokes.punchline: Pierce assumes they mean the Holocaust — not only a non sequitur but delivered with exasperated familiarity, as if Holocaust conversations are a recurring nuisance in this group.
jokes.explanation: Very Pierce — casually offensive, oblivious, and self-important. The 'you people' adds an uncomfortable layer. Works because it's character-specific and the misdirection is sharp, though it's the kind of edgy Pierce joke the show does regularly, limiting its originality.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'He barely sued me that time I ran over his foot.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is saying something ostensibly positive about Star-Burns to honor his memory.
jokes.punchline: His tribute is that Star-Burns 'barely' sued him after Pierce ran over his foot — framing restraint in litigation as the highest form of human virtue.
jokes.explanation: Economically brilliant Pierce character work. The implication that (1) Pierce casually runs over people's feet, and (2) considers low-litigiousness a character virtue reveals volumes about his sociopathic worldview. The word 'barely' does heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I just remembered I have to... feed my cat. Yeah. My cat needs feeding.

dialogue.speaker: Group
dialogue.line: You don't have a cat.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Not anymore!

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I say we honor Star-Burns by discussing him the same amount we did when he was alive.' Beat.
jokes.setup: The group is deciding how much to honor Star-Burns' memory. Jeff proposes a seemingly respectful standard.
jokes.punchline: The implied amount they discussed him while alive is essentially zero — so Jeff is suggesting they simply not discuss him at all, disguised as a tribute.
jokes.explanation: Very sharp Jeff joke. It sounds like a reasonable, even elegant proposal, but its logic collapses into 'let's ignore him' — which is both a commentary on shallow social grief and very Jeff Winger. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I think we should all remember Star-Burns as a good man. And I have proof—the restraint he showed by not suing me over that thing I did that injured him.

jokes.text: Britta being corrected mid-sentence: 'As a psychologist...' / 'Student.' / 'I hereby offer my licensed...' / 'Unlicensed.' / 'Services as a grief counselor.' / 'Grief causer.' / 'The doctor...' / 'Not even close.' / 'Is in.'
jokes.setup: Britta pompously announces her credentials and services as a grief counselor.
jokes.punchline: Each clause of her announcement is immediately corrected by others: 'psychologist' → 'student,' 'licensed' → 'unlicensed,' 'counselor' → 'causer,' 'doctor' → 'not even close.' The escalating corrections become a comedic demolition of her pretension.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed jokes. The structure is immaculate — each correction arrives precisely at the moment of maximum pomposity, and they escalate perfectly ('student' is mild correction, 'grief causer' is an actual reframe, 'not even close' is total dismissal). The joke is fully earned by Britta's character and the group's established dynamic. The rhythm is comedy-writing craft at a high level. Earns 8+ because of structural precision and near-perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We should do something to honor him. He was a great guy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I barely knew him.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Neither did I.

jokes.text: Troy calling his pen pal 'Pai Mai' mid-conversation, checking in quickly, then hanging up: 'Okay, good, I gotta go. This costs $7.'
jokes.setup: Troy is in the middle of a group discussion about grief when he suddenly makes a phone call.
jokes.punchline: He calls someone named 'Pai Mai' (presumably an exotic pen pal), confirms they're okay, and hangs up citing the $7 cost — the whole interaction is treated as completely normal and urgent.
jokes.explanation: Classic Troy non-sequitur. Works because of the unexpectedness and Troy's sincerity. The '$7' detail is a good specific grounding touch. Slightly underdeveloped — the joke could have been pushed further.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We need to call my pen pal in China to make sure he's okay.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's going to be really expensive.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know, but he's my pen pal. I have to make sure he's alive.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, there are a billion people in China.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know! That's what I'm worried about!

jokes.text: Britta dresses up as Star-Burns for grief counseling roleplay. 'For the purposes of this exercise, I am Star-Burns. Tell me the things you never got a chance to say to me.'
jokes.setup: Britta has promised grief counseling. She arrives 'prepared' — which turns out to mean she has dressed as the dead man.
jokes.punchline: The sheer earnestness of Britta's deeply misguided therapeutic approach — dressing as a dead person for psychodrama — is the joke. She's confident this is correct therapy.
jokes.explanation: Strong Britta character comedy. Her confidence in an obviously absurd therapeutic technique is perfectly in character — she's learned enough psychology to be dangerous but not enough to be competent. The visual of her in Star-Burns costume amplifies the cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I've studied psychology, biology, chemistry, and advanced neurology.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Britta, you dropped out of high school.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I studied it informally.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You watched a TED talk once.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It was a very long TED talk.

jokes.text: Group asks 'Star-Burns' (Britta): 'What's heaven like?' / 'Uh, I don't know. Glittery.'
jokes.setup: Britta has invited the group to ask 'Star-Burns' anything. She expects emotional questions.
jokes.punchline: The first question is a sincere theological inquiry about heaven, and Britta — breaking character from grief counseling into actual guessing — offers 'glittery' as a description of the afterlife.
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'glittery' as a theological answer is funny — Britta attempting to stay in character while having no idea what heaven is like, so she improvises a vague sparkly guess. Quick and effective.

jokes.text: 'Have you seen Tim Russert?' — asked of Britta-as-Star-Burns.
jokes.setup: The group is asked to ask Star-Burns meaningful, personal questions.
jokes.punchline: Pierce asks if Star-Burns has seen Tim Russert in heaven — suggesting Pierce's primary interest in the afterlife is the late NBC anchor, and treating heaven as a networking opportunity.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Pierce — his reference touchstone is a Boomer-era TV anchor, and the specificity of Tim Russert (who died in 2008) is excellent. The implication that this is Pierce's most pressing question about the afterlife is very funny and well-character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, I need your help. I'm grieving.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Really? You came to me?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, you're a psychology major.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you actually think I'm smart.

jokes.text: 'Star-Burns, I didn't know you that well, but why did you smell exactly like salami?'
jokes.setup: The group is invited to ask Star-Burns meaningful personal questions. This is supposed to be emotional catharsis.
jokes.punchline: Abed's question is not emotional or personal in the therapeutic sense — it's a specific, unanswered sensory mystery that apparently genuinely puzzled him. Delivered deadpan as if equally valid.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed. He engages with the exercise on literal rather than emotional terms — his genuine unresolved question about Star-Burns is a smell observation. The specificity of 'exactly like salami' is perfect, and the qualifier 'I didn't know you that well' mimics funeral speech structure before completely abandoning its emotional logic.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yeah, so... the afterlife is like, really bright. And there's a lot of, um, clouds? And everyone's just kind of... floating around being dead.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Britta, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, I'm not done. There's also a juice bar. Dead people love juice.

jokes.text: Troy: 'I got one. Where's my comb?' / Abed: 'I don't know.' / Troy: 'Yep, it's him.'
jokes.setup: Troy wants to verify this is really Star-Burns by asking about his comb.
jokes.punchline: Britta-as-Star-Burns doesn't know. Troy accepts this as confirmation of authenticity — apparently Star-Burns was reliably unaware of Troy's comb, and not knowing is proof of identity.
jokes.explanation: The logic is delightfully inverted — Troy validates identity through ignorance. The implication that he has a longstanding comb dispute with Star-Burns is a small, vivid bit of implied world-building. 'Yep, it's him' is perfectly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, if you can hear me, is there an afterlife?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Can you give us a sign?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, one more question: is Kent Brockman okay?

jokes.text: 'Why did you tape that switchblade to your ankle?' / 'Why did you always poop with the stall door open?'
jokes.setup: The group is warming up to the exercise and asking increasingly specific questions about Star-Burns' habits.
jokes.punchline: Two vivid, deeply specific details about Star-Burns' behavior are revealed — a switchblade ankle holster and an open-door bathroom policy — painting a portrait of a man with no social filters and unclear threat assessment.
jokes.explanation: Good world-building comedy. These questions retroactively flesh out Star-Burns as a genuinely strange person, and the escalation from dangerous (switchblade) to gross (open-door pooping) works. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Personal question to 'dead' Star-Burns... Specific and unsavory personal detail

jokes.text: 'Is it true you made out with Britta?' / Britta (as Star-Burns): 'I don't see how that's relevant.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks Star-Burns (played by Britta) if he made out with Britta — i.e., if Britta made out with herself.
jokes.punchline: Britta's refusal to engage — 'I don't see how that's relevant' — while in character confirms the rumor while maintaining therapeutic propriety. She's trying to be a counselor but is now outing her own past behavior.
jokes.explanation: Layered joke: the question puts Britta in the impossible position of answering about herself in the third person, and her deflection ('I don't see how that's relevant') is exactly what a guilty therapist would say. The structure is clever — the roleplay setup pays off in an unexpected direction.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, have you seen my comb? It's very valuable.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: No, I haven't seen it.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Star-Burns? I thought your name was Alex.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: It is. Star-Burns is just a nickname.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, I didn't know that.

jokes.text: Britta admits 'maybe it was because she was really drunk and she had just found out that her first boyfriend was getting married' — while still supposedly playing Star-Burns.
jokes.setup: Pressed about making out with Britta, 'Star-Burns' (Britta) begins to explain Britta's emotional state at the time.
jokes.punchline: Britta completely breaks the fiction of the exercise and starts defending her own past behavior from inside the character — revealing sad, specific personal context (drunk, ex getting married) in a moment of accidental oversharing.
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy. Britta's self-justification erupting through the therapeutic roleplay is both funny and genuinely revealing of her character — she's simultaneously the therapist, the patient, and the subject. The sadness of the detail ('first boyfriend was getting married') is exactly the kind of pathos-comedy balance Community does well. Earns 8+ because the construction is sophisticated and character integration is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, what was your most embarrassing moment?

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: That time I clogged the toilet at Greendale and didn't tell anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, you just told us.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: I know, I'm dead. No consequences.

jokes.text: 'Okay, grief counseling is growing on me.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has been dismissive of Britta's grief counseling from the start. The session was bizarre and nothing like actual therapy.
jokes.punchline: Jeff admits it's 'growing on him' — but only after the session devolved into embarrassing confessions about Britta's personal life. His endorsement is entirely because it was entertaining at Britta's expense.
jokes.explanation: Good Jeff character beat — his enjoyment of Britta's humiliation is very consistent, and the understatement of 'growing on me' is nicely calibrated. Functional transition joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So Britta, is it true you used to be a—

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm not talking about Belgium.

jokes.text: The Dean singing to himself in his office: '♪ Come on, I'm Dean and my hands are so clean / At this moment I am stapling ♪'
jokes.setup: We cut to the Dean's office. He is apparently singing a personalized song about his current administrative activity.
jokes.punchline: The Dean has composed a real-time musical narration of his mundane office tasks, delivered with complete sincerity. The rhyme 'clean/Dean' and the specificity of 'stapling' as a lyrical subject is absurdly self-satisfied.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dean Pelton moment. His narcissism, childlike self-satisfaction, and theatrical nature combine into an impromptu song about stapling. The specificity ('at this moment I am stapling') as a lyrical subject is what makes it. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I did not make out with Star-Burns!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, well, technically we did make out, but it was only because he said his car had a working cassette player, and I was curious about what that would be like. And it turns out it sounds exactly like you'd think—like a Walkman, but bigger. So really, I was making out with the promise of vintage audio technology, not with Star-Burns himself.

jokes.text: Dean: 'Ben, how's it deaning?' / Chang: 'Can't com-Chang.'
jokes.setup: The Dean greets Chang with a pun-greeting using his own title.
jokes.punchline: Chang responds with his own name-pun — 'can't com-Chang' as a riff on 'can't complain.' Both characters are equally delighted by wordplay at the expense of dignity.
jokes.explanation: Lightweight but pleasant wordplay exchange. 'Can't com-Chang' is the better of the two puns. The mutual delight of two power-hungry narcissists bonding over terrible puns is character-consistent. Not exceptional but lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Ow, ow, ow, ow!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is the most entertained I've been all week.

jokes.text: Dean reviewing Chang's proposal: 'Let's just give this a little look-a-roo.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is about to review a formal security proposal.
jokes.punchline: 'Look-a-roo' — a precious, babyish diminutive — is exactly the wrong register for reviewing what turns out to be a draconian security manifesto.
jokes.explanation: Small character moment. 'Look-a-roo' is a good Dean-ism, and the contrast with the seriousness of what follows gives it mild ironic weight. Functional but minor.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: ♪ I'm filing all these forms today, hip hip hooray! ♪

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: ♪ Alphabetically organized in every single way! ♪

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: ♪ Cross-referencing and collating, it's really quite fun! ♪

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: ♪ Another exciting day in the office has begun! ♪

jokes.text: Chang's security proposal includes: 'Cool new uniforms,' 'Power to enact martial law,' 'Indefinite detention, pepper spray, involuntary cavity searches... no soft-serve.'
jokes.setup: Dean reads through Chang's list of requested security powers.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from benign ('cool new uniforms') through genuinely authoritarian (martial law, indefinite detention, cavity searches) to the bathetic final item: no soft-serve. The loss of ice cream is apparently commensurate with suspension of civil liberties.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke. The structure is precisely calibrated: 'cool new uniforms' (vanity) → 'martial law' (actual dictatorship) → 'involuntary cavity searches' (rights violation) → 'no soft-serve' (petty revenge). The bathos of ending on soft-serve is what makes it exceptional, and it perfectly characterizes Chang's vanity and smallness within his megalomania. Earns high marks for structure and escalation design.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Hello, Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: That's funny, because my name is Chang, not 'Hello.'

jokes.text: Chang explains how the sausage gets made: 'It's a lot of ground meat and it gets stuffed into a casing that looks like a cross between a dude's dong and a poop.'
jokes.setup: Chang uses the cliché 'you don't want to know how the sausage gets made' to defend his authoritarian methods.
jokes.punchline: The Dean says he doesn't know how that helps him, suggesting Chang was going to explain his security methods metaphorically, but instead gave a literal, crude description of sausage production — missing the entire point of his own idiom.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of an idiom — Chang takes the metaphor completely literally and delivers a sincere, crude anatomy of sausage. 'A cross between a dude's dong and a poop' is funny in its specificity. The Dean's bewildered 'I don't know how that helps me' is the right straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We've implemented new security measures. All students must now wear ID badges at all times, submit to random bag checks, and register their vehicles with campus security.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Additionally, we're banning ice cream from all campus facilities.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I trust you all understand the severity of these measures and will comply accordingly.

jokes.text: Dean sighs about delivering bad news to Jeff's group: 'Hold my calls, I have to pick an outfit.'
jokes.setup: The Dean has just received bad news (the biology class cancellation) and must relay it. He braces himself for a difficult conversation.
jokes.punchline: His preparation is not emotional or logistical — it's sartorial. He needs to select the right outfit, suggesting this is his primary concern when facing any challenge.
jokes.explanation: Very economical Dean character beat. His vanity completely overrides the gravity of the news he has to deliver. 'Hold my calls, I have to pick an outfit' has perfect rhythm and reveals character efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I don't want to know how things work. Some things are better left a mystery.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Like sausage. You take a pig intestine, stuff it with ground meat and spices, tie it off, boil it in water until the casing splits open and reveals the steaming flesh inside.

jokes.text: Britta's grief exercise: she makes the group imagine puppies in a basket... and then the last puppy catching fire.
jokes.setup: Britta is leading the group through what begins as a standard guided visualization/emotional opening exercise.
jokes.punchline: The visualization, which started warmly with puppies, escalates to the final puppy catching fire — Britta's therapeutic technique going catastrophically off the rails.
jokes.explanation: Classic Community dark-subversive beat. The structure — set up an adorable image, single out the most vulnerable element, then burn it — is deliberate and effective. Britta's sincere commitment to this as 'necessary' makes the cringe land harder. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you just said, but it sounded disgusting.

jokes.text: 'Britta! Why are you making us feel these things?'
jokes.setup: Britta's burning-puppy visualization has provoked genuine emotional distress in the group.
jokes.punchline: Troy's anguished outcry — not anger, not pushback, but plaintive confusion at being made to feel emotions — is both funny and weirdly poignant. He's genuinely upset about the imaginary burning puppy.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. Troy's framing of emotional experience as something being done *to* him — 'making us feel these things' — is perfectly childlike and Troy-specific. High quotability because it's redeployable in almost any context where unwanted emotion is induced.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone imagine a puppy in a basket.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Now the basket is on fire.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, we're trying to process grief, not add more trauma.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: The puppy can't swim.

jokes.text: Jeff lists the five stages of grief and dares Britta: 'Name any other stage.' / 'What are you, my final?'
jokes.setup: Jeff accuses Britta of denial being the first stage of grief
jokes.punchline: Britta can't name more than one other stage and deflects with an exam analogy — revealing she doesn't know the material she's teaching
jokes.explanation: 'What are you, my final?' is a good defensive deflection that reveals Britta equates being challenged with being tested — and that she presumably doesn't do well on finals. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Why does my emotional journey always have to end with me crying in the fetal position?

jokes.text: Jeff's denial speech: 'Why not wallow for the rest of our lives and never get anything done?'... 'Or we could just admit the simple fact that one day, something is in your life and one day, it's not.'
jokes.setup: The group wants a memorial for Star-Burns; Jeff is dismissing the need for any grieving process.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'simple fact' — a deliberately evasive, abstracted way of describing death that refuses to name what has happened — is both philosophically evasive and comically vague. He's clearly in denial, and his speech about not wallowing IS his wallowing.
jokes.explanation: More character comedy than pure joke, but the irony of Jeff's denial speech being itself a form of emotional avoidance is well-calibrated. The vague abstraction ('something is in your life... it's not') lands as comedic deflection.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The five stages of grief are denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm not doing that.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What do you mean you're not doing that? It's not optional, Jeff. Everyone goes through them.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Sounds like a standardized test. I'm not great at those. I'll just skip to acceptance and we can all move on.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton bursts in singing: '♪ Dean-jour, mes amis! ♪'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just delivered a somber philosophical speech about death and impermanence. The room is emotionally tense.
jokes.punchline: The Dean arrives with a cheerful musical pun entrance ('Dean-jour' = 'Bonjour'), completely puncturing the solemnity. He is, as always, performing for an audience of himself.
jokes.explanation: 'Dean-jour, mes amis' is a solid pun that works on tone contrast alone — his cheerful irruption into grief is funny, and the multilingual self-pun ('Dean-jour') is characteristically excessive. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, actually, there are five stages of grief: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. And I'm clearly in the anger stage right now because this is a stupid question.

jokes.text: Dean announces class cancellation: '...your biology class has been can-can-cancelled.' [Chuckling]
jokes.setup: The Dean is delivering genuinely bad news — the biology class is cancelled, grades become incompletes, summer school required.
jokes.punchline: He stumbles on 'cancelled,' producing an accidental 'can-can' dance sound, then chuckles nervously. His attempt to manage the bad news delivery through charm is making it worse in real time.
jokes.explanation: Good Dean character beat — his discomfort manifesting as nervous stammering and inappropriate chuckling is very specific to him. The accidental 'can-can' is a small gem of unintended wordplay.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh, I couldn't possibly... well, if you really want me to... I suppose I could sing Ave Maria.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But only because you insisted. I mean, I've had years of training, and it would be a shame to let it go to waste...

jokes.text: Long beat of silence after the announcement that summer is gone — then a prolonged group breakdown with crying and 'No. No!' followed by the Dean's abandoned rockette kick-line.
jokes.setup: The Dean announces summer school is required due to the cancelled class. He had a 'rockette kick-line thing planned' to soften the blow.
jokes.punchline: The group's devastation is so total that it preempts the planned kick-line entirely. The Dean quietly abandons his choreography mid-crisis. The gap between his festive intentions and the actual emotional fallout is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The abandoned kick-line is a beautiful detail — the Dean prepared something festive for devastating news, and even he can tell it won't land now. The timing of the prolonged group reaction before the Dean's quiet admission is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Bonjour! It's me, Dean Pelton. I'm très Dean right now.

jokes.text: "Well, I had a little rockette kick-line thing planned, but..." — Dean's defeated acknowledgment that the room isn't in the mood
jokes.setup: Group is sobbing over the summer school news
jokes.punchline: The Dean had literally prepared a Rockettes kick-line to accompany the cancellation announcement — his showmanship persists even here
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Dean PREPARED a Rockettes number for a class cancellation announcement is perfect character comedy. The dejected 'but...' suggests he's genuinely disappointed he won't get to do it. Highest possible character integration score territory.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm afraid I have some bad news. French class has been cancelled.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: But look on the bright side — at least we can still can-can! *kicks leg*

jokes.text: Garrett's Ave Maria performance — clearly terrible based on the transcript's hesitant, broken notation: '♪ Ave ♪ ... ♪ Mariii... ♪ ... ♪ Iaaa ♪'
jokes.setup: The memorial needs music. Garrett has apparently volunteered (or been assigned) to sing Ave Maria.
jokes.punchline: What follows is clearly a catastrophic performance — the syllables are broken, stretched, and mishandled in a way that makes the transcript itself convey incompetence. The solemnity of Ave Maria is completely destroyed.
jokes.explanation: Garrett's consistent role as Greendale's most tragic, incompetent presence makes this land. The visual/audio joke can't fully register in transcript, but the broken syllabification signals a catastrophic interpretation of Schubert. Strong rewatch value as this is primarily a performance joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I was going to do a little dance number, but Annie's screaming kind of killed the vibe.

jokes.text: After Garrett finishes: 'Okay. That was Garrett singing, um, Ave Maria?' / 'Ave Maria!'
jokes.setup: Garrett finishes his terrible Ave Maria
jokes.punchline: Abed's uncertain identification of the song — delivered as a question — implies it was barely recognizable. Garrett's defensive correction is funnier still.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button. Abed's question mark on 'Ave Maria?' is devastating in its polite uncertainty — implying the song was unrecognizable. Garrett's indignant 'Ave Maria!' defense makes it a complete comedic exchange. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh no. No, no, no. After that? I'm not singing. I'm just gonna sit here and let my ears have a moment of silence.

jokes.text: Abed: 'That was Garrett singing, um, Ave Maria?' / Garrett: 'Ave Maria!'
jokes.setup: Garrett's Ave Maria concludes. Abed is emceeing the memorial.
jokes.punchline: Abed's uncertain framing ('Ave Maria?') indicates the performance was so strange he genuinely wasn't sure what he heard. Garrett's emphatic self-correction confirms: yes, it was Ave Maria, and he is proud.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Garrett performance joke. Abed's upward inflection on 'Ave Maria?' does enormous work — the question mark captures the full horror of what was just heard without elaboration. Garrett's proud 'Ave Maria!' in response adds an extra layer of tragic confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh! Because his head is shaped like a star and it's on fire!

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Oh... Because his sideburns were shaped like stars. I just got it. I just got that.'
jokes.setup: The memorial is in progress for 'Star-Burns.' Everyone has known this nickname for the entire run of the show.
jokes.punchline: Pierce has apparently gone this entire time without understanding where the nickname came from. He now connects it, in the middle of the memorial, with the wonder of genuine discovery.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode, possibly the most quotable. Pierce's slowness is a constant character trait, but the specific timing — realizing a years-long nickname's meaning at the man's memorial — is perfect. The phrasing 'I just got it. I just got that.' doubles the emphasis in a way that's both funny and sad. High quotability and rewatch value. Earns 8+ for character integration, timing, and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I've finally reached the acceptance stage. I'm at peace with who I am.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's great, Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know, right? I'm basically a Buddhist monk now.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You just got mad at a vending machine yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... different. That machine was wrong.

jokes.text: Jeff's eulogy: Greendale is 'this Fallujah of higher learning.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is giving what appears to be a standard, if edgy, eulogy at a school memorial.
jokes.punchline: He calls Greendale a 'Fallujah of higher learning' — a hyperbolic war-zone metaphor for a community college, which Britta immediately points out is a mixed metaphor.
jokes.explanation: Good Jeff rhetoric that's funny because it's immediately deflated by Britta's pedantic correction. The hyperbole is very Jeff but not among his sharpest lines.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I want to thank Greendale Community College, a school that's like a beautiful prison where the guards are also inmates, and the cafeteria food is a crime against humanity. This institution is a beacon of mediocrity in a world full of slightly better beacons. It's the participation trophy of higher education. We came here as broken people and we're leaving as slightly less broken people who now have student debt. Greendale isn't just a school, it's a cautionary tale wrapped in a school-shaped package. But somehow, against all odds and common sense, I'm going to miss this place. Because it's my cautionary tale.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Star-Burns was a hero...because he did the one thing none of us ever tried to do. He got out.' [Beat] 'And then he exploded.'
jokes.setup: Jeff builds a genuinely moving tribute — positioning Star-Burns as a hero who escaped Greendale's gravitational pull. The rhetoric escalates to an emotional peak.
jokes.punchline: 'And then he exploded' — delivered with the same rhetorical weight as the preceding lines, but completely puncturing the pathos with the blunt physical fact of the death.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode and among the stronger jokes in the series. The structure is near-perfect: Jeff's rhetoric has genuine emotional architecture, the 'He got out' is a real payoff moment, and then 'And then he exploded' destroys it with four words of brutal literalism. The beat between the lines is essential — it lets the emotional peak land before demolishing it. High impact because the joke works on the entire room as a simultaneous emotional and comedic beat. Earns 8+ on structure and economy grounds clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So Star-Burns is a hero for escaping school? That's great. What's next, we're gonna celebrate death as the ultimate escape method?

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Greendale hates its students. It sucks the lives from their bodies and forces their desiccated husks to attend summer school.' / Britta: 'Okay, Jeffrey, this is a funeral. Let's keep it light.'
jokes.setup: Jeff's eulogy has gone full nihilistic rant about Greendale.
jokes.punchline: Britta — the group's designated emotional processor — admonishes Jeff to 'keep it light' at a funeral, as if the proper register for a memorial is breezy optimism.
jokes.explanation: Britta's 'let's keep it light' is funny because it's the wrong advice for the wrong reasons — she's not wrong that Jeff is making things worse, but 'light' at a funeral is an odd goal. Good character moment, functional joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You see these? These are what summer school does to you. These are the husks of students who thought they could make it through. Look at them. Just... drained. Completely desiccated. This is what happens when the school sucks the life out of you.

jokes.text: "Annie, Annie, maybe you could say something nice about Star-Burns. Get some sugar to go with that spice."
jokes.setup: Jeff's speech has been too inflammatory; Dean tries to redirect
jokes.punchline: 'Sugar and spice' — the Dean's folksy rhyming pivot — is an absurdly cheerful way to try to rescue a funeral that's becoming a riot
jokes.explanation: The Dean's tonal obliviousness is consistent, but this specific line is less memorable than others. The 'sugar and spice' rhyme feels slightly strained.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Jeff, that was beautiful, but maybe a little dark. Could you do it again, but make it funny?

jokes.text: Annie's eulogy: 'Greendale has warped me like a Barbie in a microwave.' / 'Our school flag is an anus!'
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to offer a warmer, 'nicer' counterpoint to Jeff's nihilism at the memorial.
jokes.punchline: She starts with an extremely vivid violent simile ('Barbie in a microwave'), then caps with the blunt assertion that the school flag is an anus — both are funnier because they come from Annie, the group's most earnest member.
jokes.explanation: 'Like a Barbie in a microwave' is an exceptionally vivid, original metaphor — the specificity of Barbie (childhood, innocence, femininity) being microwaved (violated, distorted, destroyed by an institution) is both funny and genuinely dark. 'Our school flag is an anus!' is an escalation that works because (a) it's possibly true given Greendale's design sensibilities and (b) Annie screaming it at a memorial is a perfect character subversion. Combined, these lines are among the episode's best. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You know, Jeff's speech was like a soufflé - it looked impressive, but it needed a little more time in the oven. And maybe some butter. Dean Pelton always thinks everything needs more butter.

jokes.text: Response to Annie's flag claim: 'You were the guys who drew it.'
jokes.setup: Annie declares the school flag is an anus and uses it as evidence of institutional corruption.
jokes.punchline: The Dean points out that members of the study group designed it — turning Annie's accusation back on the accusers and implying the school is not to blame for their anus design.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback for fans of the show. The Dean's one-line deflection — with the implication that the study group literally drew an anus and blamed the school for displaying it — is economical and devastating. Strong rewatch/fan value.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Greendale has taken everything from me and destroyed it like a child smashing plastic toys.

jokes.text: Annie: 'We're not even the best community college in our community. Let that sink in.'
jokes.setup: Annie's escalating indictment of Greendale's institutional failures.
jokes.punchline: The superlative failure is not being the worst community college in America, but specifically being outranked within their immediate geographic area. The instruction to 'let that sink in' implies this is the most damning fact of all.
jokes.explanation: Sharp and quotable. The logic of 'not even the best in our community' is a genuinely funny precision — community college failure defined on the most local possible terms. 'Let that sink in' adds perfect deflation. Very deployable as a standalone.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Did you know our school mascot, the Human Being, was originally supposed to be called the Vagina? The university decided it was too explicit, so they changed it to something more family-friendly. But here's the thing—they didn't tell anyone! So for three years, all our uniforms, our fight song, everything said 'Go Vaginas!' before anyone noticed and we had to change it.

jokes.text: Annie: 'I'm failing a remedial biology class on a technicality, all because you don't know how to run a school.' / 'Shame on you, Dean. Shame... on... you!'
jokes.setup: Annie's speech reaches its peak indictment, addressing the Dean directly.
jokes.punchline: 'Shame... on... you!' — delivered with full melodramatic weight by Annie, complete with rhetorical pauses. The ponderous seriousness with which she executes this cliché is funnier than the words themselves.
jokes.explanation: Annie's earnest outrage applied to a low-stakes academic grievance is good character comedy. 'Edison out' (with the mic drop) below is the sharper button, but the 'Shame on you' has redeployable quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Dean, this is completely inappropriate! We can't have an anus flag!

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Annie, you were on the flag committee. You helped design it.

jokes.text: 'Edison out.' [Drops mic] [Feedback] / 'Let's maybe not drop the $50 mics, okay, guys?'
jokes.setup: Annie ends her speech with a dramatic mic drop — the classic power move.
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately grounds the drama in community college reality: they can't afford mic damage, the mic costs $50. The gesture of defiance runs directly into Greendale's budget constraints.
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic deflation. The mic drop is a power move; Abed's '$50 mic' reminder is the institutional reality check that undercuts Annie's dramatic moment while also serving as a vivid Greendale detail. The specificity of '$50' (not expensive enough to be impressive, not cheap enough to be trivial) is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: And the worst part? The absolute worst part is that nobody appreciates what I do around here. I organize the study group, I keep everyone on track, I make sure we actually learn something... and what do I get? Nothing. It's like I'm the cherry on top of a sundae, except nobody wants the cherry, they just want the ice cream, and honestly, who even puts a cherry on top of a sundae anymore? It's outdated, it's unnecessary, and frankly, it's a choking hazard.

jokes.text: Shirley's eulogy: 'Star-Burns, I'm told, was a drug dealer. Which, of course, is not good behavior. Which... but he... it was a business. Um, he had an entrepreneurial spirit. Amen.'
jokes.setup: Shirley — devout Christian, strong moral code — is supposed to say something nice at the memorial for a known drug dealer.
jokes.punchline: She navigates the theological and ethical impossibility in real time, her speech visibly collapsing as she tries to reconcile 'drug dealing' with 'something positive' and lands on 'entrepreneurial spirit.' She concludes with 'Amen' as if this was a coherent Christian tribute.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Shirley character comedy. The joke is in her real-time collision with an impossible task — eulogizing a drug dealer from a Christian framework. The stammering, the pivot to 'entrepreneurial spirit,' and the concluding 'Amen' as if the theological knot has been resolved are all perfectly calibrated. Earns 8+ on character integration grounds — nobody but Shirley could deliver this specific joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: And that's why your behavior is completely unacceptable. I'm done. Edison.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'I had dreams. Dreams of opening a sandwich shop in this cafeteria. And Greendale listened to those dreams... And stole them... And sold them to Subway.'
jokes.setup: Shirley's eulogy has drifted from Star-Burns to her own grievances. She's now eulogizing her lost business dream.
jokes.punchline: Greendale didn't just fail to support her dream — they actively sold it out to a corporate franchise. The escalation ('listened... stole... sold') and the specificity of the Subway betrayal is a vivid, funny grievance with real institutional critique underneath.
jokes.explanation: Strong character-integrated callback. The three-step structure ('listened... stole... sold') is well-crafted rhetoric, and the pivot from Star-Burns to Shirley's personal corporate betrayal is exactly the kind of self-serving grievance comedy the ensemble is built on. Fans of the season arc get extra mileage from the Subway subplot callback.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm done. I'm out.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Do you know how much these microphones cost?

jokes.text: Chang watches the riot starting: 'Yep, it'd be nice to have some protection, right? Think maybe it's about time you signed this?'
jokes.setup: The memorial has devolved into an angry mob. The Dean watches in horror.
jokes.punchline: Chang, who clearly knew this would happen (or possibly engineered it), calmly produces the security proposal the Dean previously rejected — timing it perfectly to maximize leverage.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that uses the earlier setup effectively. Chang's patient scheming — waiting for crisis to get his authoritarian powers signed — is both funny and ominous. His timing is perfect villain comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I had a dream of owning my own sandwich shop. A place where I could serve my community, where every sandwich was made with love and care. But then Subway came to town with their corporate machinery, their massive resources, their ability to undercut my prices. They didn't just take my business—they took my dream.

jokes.text: Dean: 'Just promise me you'll use restraint.' / Chang: 'Yep. Every type we got.'
jokes.setup: The Dean agrees to sign Chang's security proposal but asks for restraint in its use.
jokes.punchline: Chang interprets 'restraint' physically — as in physical restraints (zip ties, handcuffs, etc.) — and assures the Dean they have every kind. The word means something completely different to each party.
jokes.explanation: Excellent wordplay joke with genuine menace underneath. 'Every type we got' is funny on the surface, chilling on reflection — Chang already has an inventory of physical restraints prepared. The double meaning is clean, the economy is perfect, and it characterizes both the Dean's obliviousness and Chang's premeditation. Earns 8+ on structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: This funeral is depressing.

jokes.text: Chang to his security team: 'This is the day we've been waiting for. Suit... up!' [All cheer]
jokes.setup: Chang is being given official security powers at a community college during a minor protest.
jokes.punchline: His address to his child army is pitched at the level of a general rallying troops before a major battle — the disproportionality between register and situation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Functional Chang grandiosity joke. The 'Suit... up!' is a recognizable dramatic beat (How I Met Your Mother) used here to underscore the absurdity of Chang's self-importance. Works but doesn't rise above competent.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Chang, I need you to show some restraint.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You got it, Dean. I'll use the leather cuffs. Or maybe the chains. Ooh, or that fuzzy handcuff thing from the party store!

jokes.text: The riot chant: '♪ When I say Greendale, you say sucks / Greendale — Sucks ♪'
jokes.setup: A school protest/riot is breaking out at a memorial that became a grievance rally.
jokes.punchline: The chant is a simple call-and-response perfectly calibrated to mob dynamics — but the content is specifically targeted at the institution hosting the riot, making the students literally be their own worst advertisement.
jokes.explanation: Funny in context — a school's own students leading a 'your school sucks' chant at a school-sanctioned event. Not the most sophisticated joke in the episode but lands as a crowd moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You will address me as 'Sir' or 'Lord Chang.' Failure to comply will result in demerits.

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard (Child)
dialogue.line: Yes, Lord Chang!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Excellent. Now, who wants to help me reorganize the campus into a militaristic state with me as supreme leader?

dialogue.speaker: Security Guards (Children)
dialogue.line: We do, Lord Chang! All hail Chang! All hail Chang!

jokes.text: Leonard's speech: 'As a student who's been at Greendale for over a decade, I think I've earned the right to say a few final words.' / Crowd: 'Let him talk!' / Leonard: 'Let's burn this mother down!'
jokes.setup: Leonard — a very old recurring student who has clearly been at Greendale extremely long — commands the crowd's respect with his credentials.
jokes.punchline: The 'few final words' the crowd is invested in are simply an incitement to arson, delivered with gleeful abandon. His long tenure at Greendale has produced no wisdom, just grievance.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and an excellent Leonard character moment. The structure is perfect: the gravitas of his credentials ('over a decade'), the crowd's investment ('let him talk!'), and then the complete betrayal of their expectations with 'Let's burn this mother down!' The joke earns its punchline because Leonard's characterization (aging, petty, nihilistic recurring student) makes this exact outcome feel inevitable while still being surprising. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: You know, Charles Manson said something that really applies here...

dialogue.speaker: Multiple
dialogue.line: [crowd erupts in chaos and rioting]

jokes.text: During the riot: 'I'm gonna take everything but onions and olives. I know my comb's in here, you son of a bitch!'
jokes.setup: The riot is in full chaos. Various people are ransacking things. Troy is in action.
jokes.punchline: Troy's riot activity is (1) selectively looting a food station while expressing condiment preferences, and (2) looking for his comb — the same comb he asked about during the grief counseling session. His priorities in a riot are perfectly Troy.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and character integration. Troy's riot behavior — discriminating food looting (no onions or olives) and comb-seeking — is perfectly in character and pays off the earlier comb joke. 'You son of a bitch' addressed to an inanimate storage location is a great detail. Earns 8+ on character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm not looting for TVs or jewelry. I'm going straight for the organic, free-range, artisanal section.

jokes.text: 'Look, tiny riot gear. Aww.'
jokes.setup: Chang's security force confronts the rioters. We suddenly see the security force is children in miniature riot gear.
jokes.punchline: Annie's response — 'Aww' — treats the terrifying presence of a riot squad as an adorable surprise, because the gear is tiny and therefore cute, even as it's about to be deployed against her.
jokes.explanation: Excellent visual gag with a perfect one-word button. The reveal of child soldiers in tiny riot gear is inherently funny; Annie's 'Aww' is the ideal Annie response — she can't not find children cute, even in riot suppression. 'Tiny riot gear' as a phrase is highly quotable. Earns 8+ on economy (three words carry the full visual joke) and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Has anyone seen my comb? My hair is completely out of control!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I don't care if there's a riot going on, a man's got to have his standards.

jokes.text: Post-pepper-spray: 'It's so peppery!'
jokes.setup: Chang's child army deploys pepper spray on the rioters. Someone is pepper-sprayed.
jokes.punchline: The victim's description of pepper spray — 'it's so peppery!' — is a hilariously mild and culinarily-framed response to chemical irritant. They've essentially described it as a condiment rather than a weapon.
jokes.explanation: Very funny one-liner. The literal description of pepper spray as 'peppery' — treating a chemical weapon like a food experience — is a perfect deflation. High quotability. Slight character integration penalty for being unattributed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh my god, look at these tiny handcuffs. They're so cute!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And this little belt with all the equipment... I can't even...

jokes.text: Security guard to Jeff: 'Strange, I'm not finding any pepper spray on you.' / Jeff: 'Well, check harder.' / 'It's not like I'm crying because I was chased by the gang of scary 12-year-olds.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is apparently crying and being searched for pepper spray by a guard.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's emphatic denial — 'check harder' — when no pepper spray is found, followed by the defensive disclaimer that he's definitely not crying because of the 12-year-olds, is a classic 'doth protest too much' construction. He was clearly both pepper-sprayed and emotionally affected by child soldiers chasing him.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's vanity and pride making him deny being physically bested by children is very character-specific. 'Scary 12-year-olds' is a great phrase because 'scary' and '12-year-olds' don't belong together, but in this context they do. Good structure on the double denial.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not intimidated by children! I just... I don't like their energy.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'How about Pierce Hawthorne and the Greendale Six?' / Someone: 'Pierce!' / Pierce: 'How about the Greendale Five?'
jokes.setup: The Dean tells them they'll be known as the 'Greendale Seven' — a potentially cool designation. The group takes a beat to appreciate it.
jokes.punchline: Pierce tries to rebrand the group name to center himself, and when that's rejected, immediately offers to remove another person — suggesting he would happily expel a friend for a better-sounding name credit.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pierce character joke. His immediate pivot from 'put my name on it' to 'cut someone else out' when the first gambit fails is both funny and revealing — he genuinely considers his branding needs more important than group solidarity. The escalation (Seven → Hawthorne and Six → Five) is clean and fast. High character integration score. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: The Greendale Seven? I like it. Very Lord of the Rings.

jokes.text: Annie: 'I'm such a bad Dean.' / Jeff: 'No, you're not.' / Britta: 'Well, you are. But... we're worse students.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is blaming himself. Jeff immediately denies this. Britta steps in.
jokes.punchline: Britta agrees the Dean IS a bad Dean — correcting Jeff's knee-jerk reassurance — but then pivots to frame the group as even worse students, which is meant to be comforting and fails at that too.
jokes.explanation: Good Britta moment — her 'well, you are' agreement is the kind of blunt honesty she mistakes for emotional intelligence. The structure of affirmation-correction-attempted-comfort is nicely delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Greendale Seven? What about me? I'm part of this group.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, you are part of the group.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Yeah, but the name doesn't have me in it. It should be the Greendale Eight. Or better yet, Pierce's Seven. That way everyone knows I'm the leader.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'We trashed the school like a TV commercial where the teacher banned skittles.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to describe how disproportionate the group's reaction was.
jokes.punchline: The reference point for maximum school chaos is a 'TV commercial where the teacher banned skittles' — evoking a very specific genre of candy advertisement where prohibition leads to absurd rebellion. It's self-aware media literacy applied to real events.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-observational joke that uses a hyper-specific pop-culture touchstone (the school-rebellion candy commercial genre) as a point of reference. Very Jeff — he understands the narrative shape of their behavior in cultural terms.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, what if we lower it to 40?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: No wait, 35.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Actually, let's go with 30.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'That's sweet of you to say, Jeffrey. But it doesn't change the fact that we're all Ted Danson at Whoopie Goldberg's roast.'
jokes.setup: The group is trying to make the Dean feel better. The Dean has accepted partial blame.
jokes.punchline: The Dean evokes the infamous 1993 Friar's Club Roast incident where Ted Danson appeared in blackface — using it as a metaphor for 'we did something well-intentioned that was actually horrifying and cannot be undone.' The specificity and unexpectedness of this reference is startling.
jokes.explanation: Very specific, unexpected reference that works because it's exactly right — the Ted Danson/Whoopi Goldberg roast is the perfect cultural shorthand for 'we meant well but caused a spectacle.' The Dean using it shows surprising cultural literacy (or at least pop-culture scandal retention) and makes the metaphor both funny and apt. The originality of the reference choice is the joke's main strength.

jokes.text: Annie: 'What if we all back each other up and explain we were experiencing funeral crazies? I can say that's a thing because I'm a psych major.'
jokes.setup: Group needs a legal/institutional strategy for their board hearing
jokes.punchline: Annie invents 'funeral crazies' as a clinical defense and validates it with her own psych major status — a Britta-level credential overclaim
jokes.explanation: 'Funeral crazies' as a clinical term is funny; Annie using her psych major to validate her own made-up diagnosis is a callback to Britta's credential overclaiming (joke 16) but applied to Annie's earnest problem-solving mode. Good.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I feel terrible about this situation. You know, it reminds me of that time I did the roast and it was... well, let's just say I've made some choices I'm not proud of.

jokes.text: Annie suggests blaming Chang: 'How about the crazy man who commanded a bunch of preteens to spray poison in our faces?' / Jeff: 'You know what? It was right under our noses, wasn't it?'
jokes.setup: The group is looking for a fall guy. Annie makes a reasonable case for blaming Chang.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'right under our noses' is a pun on 'obvious' (idiom) + the pepper spray actually being deployed near their noses (literal). The double meaning — it was obvious AND it was literally at nose level — is a wordplay joke delivered as if Jeff just realized something profound.
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-timed pun that works better than most Community wordplay because the double meaning is genuinely earned by context (pepper spray to the face) rather than forced. Jeff's delivery of it as an insight lands the joke properly.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Come on, group hug!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Pass.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm good.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not happening.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Maybe later, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I think I'm coming down with something.

jokes.text: Group hug: 'Group hug... where I'm between Jeff and Troy.' / 'Here we go... oop, you're walking away from the hug.'
jokes.setup: The Dean calls for a group hug after the emotional crisis.
jokes.punchline: The Dean has specific positioning requirements for the group hug (between Jeff and Troy), which betrays his attraction to both of them. He immediately announces others are walking away, leaving him embracing no one.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton character beat — his attraction to Jeff and Troy is a running character note, and his transparent positioning within the hug is both funny and sad. 'Oop, you're walking away from the hug' as a resigned observation is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Tomorrow? More like... tomorry.

jokes.text: Dean: 'I regret giving you that unasked for adult back rub when you were asleep that once.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is confessing regrets to Chang as he prepares to fire him — escalating from professional regrets (powers, child army) to personal ones.
jokes.punchline: Among his professional regrets, he includes giving Chang an unsolicited back rub while Chang slept — an act that is simultaneously deeply inappropriate and somehow the least of their problems. The 'that once' implies he's counted carefully.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark escalation in the Dean's list of regrets. 'Unasked for adult back rub when you were asleep' is funny because (1) the descriptor 'adult' implies it needed to be distinguished from some other kind, (2) 'that once' is a nervous qualifier that suggests he's tracked the incident, and (3) it's framed as a professional regret alongside martial law. The specificity is what makes it.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I have some regrets about Chang. Serious regrets. I may have enabled his worst impulses because I was afraid of him, and I may have also found him attractive in ways that confuse me.

jokes.text: News report: 'The single worst wake riot this district has ever seen. And we've seen our share.'
jokes.setup: Local news is covering the Greendale riot
jokes.punchline: 'We've seen our share' — implying multiple wake riots have occurred in this district, normalizing something completely abnormal
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan news anchor joke. The implication of multiple wake riots is a good background absurdism about Greendale's neighborhood/district. 'And we've seen our share' is the punchline — world-weary acceptance of wake riots as a local phenomenon.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I have some regrets about Chang. Extremely inappropriate past behavior.

jokes.text: School board hearing: Chang arrives with cookies, glad-handing board members, remembering cookie preferences: 'I never forget a face or a favorite cookie.'
jokes.setup: The Greendale Seven are facing a formal school board hearing for the riot. Chang enters in disguise as a reasonable, helpful figure.
jokes.punchline: Chang's cookie-bringing, face-remembering, 'I never forget a favorite cookie' persona is a perfect parody of institutional ass-covering — using folksy warmth to launder authoritarian behavior.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chang character work. 'I never forget a face or a favorite cookie' is a great line — the cookie specificity makes the manipulation more vivid. Chang pivoting from warlord to folksy bureaucrat is funny and slightly disturbing, as intended.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Dean Pelton, meet Dean Pelton.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: What?! That's impossible!

dialogue.speaker: Fake Dean
dialogue.line: Hello, Dean.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: No, no, no, this can't be happening!

jokes.text: Jeff's outburst: 'Chang is a psychopathic wannabe warlord with an army of prepubescent thugs. He was living in the school's air vent system with a monkey!'
jokes.setup: Jeff watches the school board buy Chang's act completely. He snaps and tries to tell the truth.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's list of Chang's actual crimes escalates perfectly: psychopath → warlord → child army → air vent residence → monkey. Each element is true and each is more bizarre than the last. The monkey detail is the peak of absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Strong escalation joke that also rewards longtime viewers who know the air vent/monkey backstory. The list structure is well-calibrated — 'prepubescent thugs' is a good phrase, and the matter-of-fact addition of 'with a monkey' as the final escalation is excellent bathos. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: What is this?! What are you doing in my office dressed like me?!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Dean, I can explain—

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: No! No, you listen here. You think you can just waltz in here, put on my cardigan, my ascot, and— Do you have any idea what I've built here? This institution, this legacy, and you're standing there looking like some cheap knockoff of perfection! I'm going to have you expelled so fast your head will spin, and then I'm going to— I'm going to—

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh my God. You actually look good in that.

jokes.text: Board hearing: Dean Pelton rushes in. 'Hey guys. Can't stay, gotta run, but, uh, these troublemakers have got to go.'
jokes.setup: Dean appears at the hearing — presumably to defend the students or explain the context
jokes.punchline: He breezes in, dismisses the group as 'troublemakers,' and leaves — revealing he's been replaced/turned by Chang
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the Dean appears to be a savior, 'can't stay, gotta run' subverts expectations completely, and 'these troublemakers have got to go' is a betrayal delivered with casual breeziness. Good economy in a plot-carrying moment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'd like to address the school board about the loss of a classmate today.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: His name was Señor Lizardo, and he was a bearded dragon. He was a good pet.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: He will be missed.

jokes.text: Board Member: 'I've heard enough... May God have mercy on your souls.' / Expels all seven.
jokes.setup: The school board hearing has concluded. Chang has charmed the board with cookies while the group has made increasingly unhinged arguments.
jokes.punchline: 'May God have mercy on your souls' — a phrase reserved for death sentences — applied to community college expulsion. The register is completely wrong for the punishment, which makes it funny.
jokes.explanation: Good bathos joke — death-sentence gravity applied to academic discipline. Works because of the contrast, though it's a fairly standard register-mismatch joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I brought cookies for the board members.

dialogue.speaker: Board Member
dialogue.line: That's very thoughtful, Mr. Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Yes, well, last time someone stole them, so I'm keeping my eye on you, Gerald.

jokes.text: Post-expulsion: 'Rusty bucket? Rusty bucket? / Rusty bucket? — Yep. / Okay, transform and roll out.'
jokes.setup: The group has just been expelled. The audience expects despair or processing of the news.
jokes.punchline: Troy and Abed execute a prearranged code phrase and response ('Rusty bucket') that apparently triggers an Transformers-style dispersal signal ('Transform and roll out'). They had a contingency for expulsion, which suggests they expected it.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Troy and Abed moment. The existence of a pre-planned expulsion protocol — with code phrase AND Transformers-style disbanding signal — is perfect for these two characters. It implies they've planned for this exact scenario, which is both endearing and absurd. 'Transform and roll out' as the actual command to leave a school hearing earns the laugh. Earns 8+ on character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: How's the hearing going?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Not great. I think we might riot.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: At your own hearing?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're not great at focusing our anger.

jokes.text: Pierce: '13 years of college down the drain. I was gonna be the first one in my family to graduate from community college. Everyone else graduated from normal college. Now they're really gonna give me a hard time.'
jokes.setup: The group processes their expulsion. Pierce reflects on what he's lost.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's planned distinction — 'first in family to graduate from community college' — when his family already has normal college degrees is both a commentary on his diminished expectations and a vivid portrait of his status anxiety. 'They're really gonna give me a hard time' is the button.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. The inverse achievement — being the first to reach a lesser educational bar when your family has already surpassed it — is a precise and funny observation about Pierce's life trajectory. 'Now they're really gonna give me a hard time' implies this is his PRIMARY concern post-expulsion, not the expulsion itself. Earns 8+ on character integration and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang, where exactly are you living right now?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm living in the school's air vents. They're rent-free and have excellent acoustics.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're living in the air vents. Of a school.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Yes. I've decorated with things I've found. There's a motivational poster, and a binder full of classified documents I found in the dean's office.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Yeah, well, my life can't get double ruined.' (While drinking.)
jokes.setup: Someone notices Jeff is drinking. He explains why.
jokes.punchline: 'My life can't get double ruined' — the logical reasoning that if things are already maximally bad, additional risk is irrelevant. The phrase 'double ruined' as if ruin has measurable units is funny.
jokes.explanation: 'Double ruined' is a great coinage — the application of quantitative logic to ruin is funny and Jeff-appropriate. Very quotable and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Fake Dean
dialogue.line: Well, I have to say, I'm very disappointed in all of you. This kind of behavior is exactly what's wrong with students today.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Whatever, I'm the worst.' / Jeff: 'I'm also the worst.' / Shirley: 'Not gonna argue, but I am gonna forgive you.'
jokes.setup: Britta is being self-flagellating. Jeff agrees he's also the worst, as a form of camaraderie.
jokes.punchline: Shirley doesn't dispute that they're the worst — she agrees implicitly — but pivots to Christian forgiveness anyway. 'Not gonna argue' is the key beat: she confirms the judgment before offering the grace.
jokes.explanation: Very precise Shirley character joke. The sequence — 'not gonna argue' (damning agreement) + 'but I am gonna forgive you' (Christian magnanimity) — is a perfect character beat. Shirley's faith is consistent but her social honesty cuts through the piety.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what the worst part about going to community college is? It's not the education, it's not the facilities, it's knowing that somewhere out there, my father is looking down from heaven, shaking his head in disappointment.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Roll a die to see who gets it?' (For pizza door duty, post-expulsion.)
jokes.setup: The doorbell rings and someone needs to get the pizza. Normal people would just go get it.
jokes.punchline: Abed suggests settling pizza-door duty with a die roll — a reference to the show's earlier 'darkest timeline' episode where a die roll determined fates. For Abed, the die is always the right governance mechanism.
jokes.explanation: Deep callback for Community fans — Abed suggesting the die for a mundane decision is a callback to the most celebrated episode of the series. Works on two levels: character (Abed's rules-based thinking) and meta (acknowledging the callback structure of the episode's ending).

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, I could have gone to a real university. But nooo, I had to come here to Greendale. Do you know what that means? Community college would have been my family's lowest achievement.

jokes.text: Abed: 'I assumed this was the best timeline, but what if it's the darkest?'
jokes.setup: Abed is reflecting on the night's events. He uses the established 'darkest timeline' framework from the show's own mythology.
